#4350. Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

Toyota is getting into electric bikes. Well, sort of.

The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.

And when Toyota says compact, it means it. The little electric ride can reportedly fold up in around 30 seconds and become small enough to fit inside the trunk of the brand’s GR86 sports car. Think of it like Toyota’s take on the Motocompacto.

The BKE Concept was unveiled as part of the newly revived Scion by Toyota brand, which the company is positioning less as the return of the quirky youth-oriented car brand many Americans remember and more as a sort of experimental mobility laboratory.

Toyota calls the new Scion a “freedom lab” where the company can explore vehicles and mobility concepts that don’t necessarily fit neatly into its conventional automotive lineup. Alongside the BKE, Toyota showed its KEI-01 ultra-compact utility truck and a hybrid side-by-side.

But perhaps unsurprisingly for me, it’s the tiny electric two-wheeler that caught my attention.

And I should point out here that while Toyota refers to it as an “electric bike” in its own brand literature, the lack of pedals means that the cute little two-wheeler is not going to qualify as an electric bicycle in Europe or North America. The moniker means it merely slots into the broader electric bike category that encompasses everything from electric bicycles to scooters and motorcycles. In essence, the BKE is more or less a small seated e-scooter, sometimes referred to as a “no-ped”.

Despite looking like the kind of concept vehicle that might have been whipped up for an auto show, Toyota says the BKE has actually been under development for several years.

A small team of chassis and electrical engineers has reportedly been testing and refining the design based on real-world use and feedback.

The basic idea came from a fairly simple question: How could Toyota make short-distance mobility easier and integrate it more seamlessly into everyday life?

The result is essentially a secondary vehicle designed to travel inside your primary vehicle.

Toyota specifically highlights camping, errands, last-mile transportation, and even using the BKE as a pit bike alongside a GR86. The bike can also be recharged from the 110V AC outlets found in many Toyota vehicles, meaning the car carrying it can effectively serve as its mobile charging station.

Believe it or not, Toyota Chairman Akio Toyoda has apparently been involved in the testing process himself. Toyoda attracted attention after riding a similar small electric mobility device around the 2025 Japan Mobility Show, and Toyota says his experience riding prototypes has even resulted in design changes.

After Toyoda complained about getting splashed while riding through puddles, for example, engineers enlarged the rear fender.

It’s a small detail, but it’s also a pretty textbook example of Toyota’s famous kaizen philosophy of continuous improvement.

Here’s where things get a little frustrating for those of us who want to know what the BKE can actually do.

Toyota hasn’t announced the motor power, battery capacity, range, top speed, or even the vehicle’s weight. There’s also no pricing because, for now, there’s nothing to buy.

Toyota is referring to the BKE strictly as a concept and hasn’t announced production plans or a timetable for bringing it to market.

But the fact that Toyota says a small engineering team has spent several years developing and testing the BKE makes it more interesting than your typical one-off styling exercise.

And the underlying idea makes a lot of sense.

I’m obviously a big believer in matching the vehicle to the trip. Taking a 4,000-pound car several miles to move one person isn’t always the most efficient solution, and a compact electric two-wheeler gives drivers an easy way to leave the larger vehicle behind for those shorter trips.

Toyota itself makes essentially the same argument, saying that using smaller vehicles for shorter journeys could reduce emissions by better matching the vehicle to the task.

There’s also something amusingly circular about one of the world’s largest automakers arriving at the conclusion that sometimes the best vehicle for a trip is a tiny electric bike.

But hey, I’ll take it. Now Toyota just needs to actually build the thing – and preferably tell us how fast it goes first.

#4349. Scientists create a remarkable new rechargeable battery using vitamin B12

Scientists have found an unexpected new use for vitamin B12, a nutrient best known for its importance to human health. Researchers at the University of Córdoba have incorporated the vitamin into a rechargeable battery, demonstrating for the first time that it can serve as a catalyst in this type of energy storage system.

Vitamin B12 is essential for normal bodily function and is naturally present in animal products. The vitamin is produced by certain bacteria, which occur in nature and are also grown commercially to supply the food and pharmaceutical industries. In addition to its established applications in medicine, nutrition, and veterinary care, B12 is used to address certain nutritional deficiencies. It has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because of its potential to help reduce fatigue.

Now, scientists are exploring an entirely different application. By using the vitamin to support the chemical reactions inside a battery, they have developed a prototype capable of completing up to 250 charging and discharging cycles.

How Vitamin B12 Makes a Rechargeable Battery Possible

The new battery was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba's Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). It uses zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air to produce electricity, with vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, playing a crucial role in the process.

To make the design work, the researchers attached vitamin B12 molecules to single-walled carbon nanotubes. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its center, which helps drive the electrochemical reactions needed for the battery to function.

The team has previously experimented with natural molecules as battery catalysts, including hemoglobin and catalase. These substances contain iron (II) and iron (III), respectively. Vitamin B12 represents the group's third effort to use a biological molecule for this purpose, but it has delivered an important advance: a battery that can be recharged repeatedly, completing as many as 250 cycles.

One of the biggest obstacles was keeping vitamin B12 inside the battery. Because the vitamin dissolves readily in water, it would normally be difficult to retain in a system that relies on a water-based electrolyte.

The researchers overcame this problem by securing the vitamin to carbon nanotubes, using an approach inspired by how amino acids connect to form proteins.

Manuel Cano Luna, one of the study's authors, explained that "we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries," while describing the team's search for useful biological compounds.

Their attachment technique imitates "the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins."

Alongside Cano Luna, the research team included Valentín García Caballero, Miguel López León, Pablo Gómez Argudo, Luis Camacho Delgado, José Miguel Rodríguez Mellado, María Teresa Martín Romero, José Abad López, and Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero.

A Safer, Lighter Alternative to Lithium-Ion Batteries

The findings, published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A, could contribute to the development of battery technologies that depend less on the materials used in conventional lithium-ion batteries.

Although lithium-ion batteries are widely used, obtaining their raw materials can involve significant economic, environmental, and social challenges. Zinc-air batteries offer a potential alternative because they can store substantial amounts of energy relative to their weight while relying on materials that are more readily available.

Zinc is abundant and recyclable, and these batteries use oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere as part of their energy-producing reactions. Because they draw oxygen from the air rather than storing all the necessary reactants internally, they can also be lighter than other battery designs.

This advantage has helped make zinc-air batteries increasingly useful in compact electronic devices, particularly hearing aids. Another benefit is their use of non-flammable, water-based electrolytes, which can reduce fire risks and improve safety.

A major challenge in developing rechargeable zinc-air batteries is finding a catalyst that can efficiently support the chemical reactions involved in both producing and storing electricity.

During discharge, the battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Recharging requires the relevant chemical reactions to proceed in the opposite direction. A suitable catalyst must therefore be effective in both processes.

According to researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero, vitamin B12 "has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen."

This ability to support both reactions is what makes the vitamin particularly promising for rechargeable zinc-air battery technology.

Could Vitamin B12 Help Store Renewable Energy?

The successful prototype offers a new direction for researchers seeking affordable, sustainable alternatives to existing energy storage technologies.

If the approach can be developed further, batteries using vitamin B12 catalysts could eventually help address one of the biggest challenges facing renewable energy: storing excess electricity generated by sources such as solar and wind power for use when production falls.

Although the technology remains at the research stage, demonstrating up to 250 charge and discharge cycles shows that a familiar biological molecule can play an unexpected role in rechargeable battery design. The discovery adds to growing efforts to use naturally occurring substances to create safer, lighter, and more sustainable ways to store energy.

#4347. Tesla Cybertruck’s already impressive turning radius gets even tighter

Tesla is rolling out an update that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.

But there’s a catch. It only works on 2027 model year Cybertrucks, and Tesla plans to stop building the truck by the end of next summer.

Tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path. “Even tighter turns now rolling out to new Cybertrucks,” the account wrote.

In a follow-up post, Tesla said the improvement requires software version 2026.44 or newer and “only applies to model year 2027 Cybertrucks.”

It's not the size … it's how you maneuver itEven tighter turns now rolling out to new Cybertrucks pic.twitter.com/FuNoox4ax0

Tesla didn’t share a new turning circle figure. In the video, the “after” circle is visibly smaller than the “before” one by what looks to be at least a foot.

The Cybertruck’s maneuverability comes from its rear-wheel steering paired with steer-by-wire. At low speeds, the rear wheels turn opposite to the fronts, which shrinks the space the truck needs to make a U-turn. We’ve been tracking the Cybertruck’s four-wheel steering since the prototype days, when Tesla was showing it off in parking garages.

Even before this update, the results were impressive. Tesla’s owner’s manual lists the Cybertruck’s curb-to-curb turning circle at about 43.5 ft (13.25 m). That beats the Ford F-150 Lightning at roughly 47.8 ft and the Rivian R1T at 44.9 ft, and it’s within about 4 ft of a Model Y. Not bad for a 6,600-lb truck that’s nearly 19 feet long.

And Tesla always said there was more to come. At launch, the rear wheels turned only about 3 degrees. In early 2024, a Tesla engineer said a software update would push that to 10 degrees, and Elon Musk said the company had improvements in the works to “tighten the turning circle significantly.”

Tesla hasn’t said whether this update delivers the full 10 degrees, or why it’s limited to 2027 trucks. If it comes down to hardware, owners of earlier Cybertrucks who were counting on this as an over-the-air upgrade are out of luck.

Credit where it’s due. The turning circle is one of the best things about the Cybertruck, and anyone who has driven one knows it. Steer-by-wire combined with rear-wheel steering is real engineering, and other vehicles are just starting to get that combo a couple years after Cybertruck had it. Making it even better is a nice update.

And 39.4 feet turning circle for the Cadillac Escalade which also has rear wheel steering. As does the iX5 (39.7'), MB GLC (36.7') and EQS (35.8'), the Lucid Gravity (38.4), Hummer 37.4', Cayenne (38.4) and a around two dozen other vehicles on the market today. So maybe this is not such big news after all?

Earlier this month, Musk announced that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas to make room for Cybercab. He has since pushed the end date to the end of summer 2027 to work through an “order backlog.” We estimate Tesla is delivering about 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks a quarter, roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year it planned for.

So Tesla is improving a 2027 model year truck that it will stop making next summer. And since Tesla now only sells the $109,990 Cyberbeast, the people getting this upgrade are the few still buying the most expensive Cybertruck in its final months. It does nothing about what actually sank the truck: pricing that never came close to the $39,900 promised in 2019, range and towing that fell short, and a design most truck buyers never warmed up to.

It’s a cool engineering flex on a product with an expiration date. If Tesla had delivered this kind of polish on the $40,000 truck it promised, would we be writing the Cybertruck’s obituary right now?

Lord of Hatred may finally make good on the Mephisto arc of Diablo 4's campaign, which started in the original game and carried through Vessel of Hatred.

Very much when we expected it, Blizzard has officially revealed Diablo 4’s next major expansion at The Game Awards. Lord of Hatred delivers a new campaign that continues the mainline story, picking up from where Vessel of Hatred left off. Mephisto, the eponymous Lord of Hatred, has seemingly finally escaped imprisonment to rule over Sanctuary.

Lord of Hatred is the second Diablo 4 expansion, and it will be available on PC, PS5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S on April 28.

It’s always a big deal when we get a new Diablo expansion, especially for a game as starved of fresh (major) content as Diablo 4 has been. But perhaps the biggest piece of news out of the Lord of Hatred reveal is that the expansion is bringing not one, but two new classes to the game.

The first of which is The Paladin, whereas the second is being kept under wraps. Even more surprising is that The Paladin is playable right now for anyone who pre-purchases the expansion. This is a well-timed shadow drop, especially given that Diablo 4’s latest season has just kicked off.

Beyond itemisation, each class’ skill tree will grow with new bonus skill variants. In fact, the entire skill system is being reworked for all classes - though details are a little sparse at the moment.

You can also expect the level cap to go up, which is very likely necessary to fit all the new skills and various systems. Blizzard offered a deep dive into the new Paladin class, which you see on the official blog.

#4344. Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer

Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life. The discovery, made by researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC), could help doctors identify families with a heightened genetic risk and detect cancer before it spreads.

Most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time. However, approximately 5% to 10% are associated with inherited mutations that can be passed from parents to their children, creating a cancer risk that may extend across generations.

Among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These inherited changes can substantially raise the likelihood of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Testing for BRCA mutations has reshaped cancer prevention and treatment by allowing people with elevated risks to receive earlier screening and preventive care.

Now, a study published in Cancer Discovery points to another gene, CDK12, as a potentially important marker of inherited prostate cancer risk. After examining genetic information from more than 4,500 people with aggressive prostate cancer, the researchers discovered five unrelated men with inherited mutations in CDK12. Every one of these men developed metastatic prostate cancer between ages 44 and 62, meaning the cancer had spread beyond the prostate.

"What's striking is that every patient we identified with this inherited mutation had already developed metastatic disease by the time they were diagnosed," said senior author Dr. Alexander Wyatt, associate professor of urologic sciences in the UBC faculty of medicine and UBC President's Excellence Chair in Precision Oncology. "The opportunity now is to identify these families earlier and give people the chance to benefit from enhanced screening, when there are still curative treatment options."

A Hidden Genetic Cause of Aggressive Prostate Cancer

The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about CDK12. Scientists previously believed that harmful changes in this gene developed spontaneously inside cancer cells rather than being inherited from a parent.

To investigate whether the inherited mutations were actually contributing to the disease, the team examined the patients' tumors for a distinctive pattern of genetic damage associated with loss of CDK12 function. This molecular fingerprint helped connect the inherited mutations to the development of their cancers.

"The tumors provided us with a genetic signature that pointed directly back to CDK12," said lead author Dr. Sofie Tolmeijer, a postdoctoral fellow in the Wyatt lab. "It gave us compelling evidence that these inherited mutations were playing a direct role in causing their cancer."

The findings emerged from a broad international research effort involving UBC, BC Cancer, the Vancouver Coastal Health Research Institute, and the University of Washington, along with scientists at institutions in Australia, the Netherlands, Spain, and Belgium.

Despite the potentially serious consequences, inherited CDK12 mutations appear to be exceptionally uncommon. The researchers found them in approximately one out of every 1,000 people with aggressive prostate cancer. Even at that low frequency, they estimate that hundreds of families around the world could be affected.

"While this mutation is extremely rare, the discovery could be lifesaving for the families who carry it," said Dr. Tolmeijer. "Finding one person with an inherited mutation gives us the opportunity to identify other family members at risk and help them take action before cancer develops or spreads."

Genetic Testing Could Help Detect Prostate Cancer Earlier

One of the most promising implications of the discovery is that doctors may not need to develop entirely new testing technology to put the findings into practice.

The researchers recommend including CDK12 in standard genetic testing panels used to assess hereditary prostate cancer risk. These panels examine multiple genes associated with inherited cancer susceptibility, helping identify individuals who may benefit from closer medical monitoring.

Importantly, the clinical technology required to detect CDK12 mutations already exists. That could make expanding genetic testing relatively straightforward, potentially reducing the time and expense needed to bring the discovery into routine patient care.

"One of the most exciting aspects of this discovery is that we already have the technology needed to act on it," said Dr. Wyatt, who is also a senior research scientist at the Vancouver Prostate Centre and senior scientist at BC Cancer. "Adding CDK12 to existing genetic tests is relatively straightforward, which means this discovery could move from the research lab into clinical care much more quickly."

Could the Same Mutation Increase Ovarian Cancer Risk?

The study also uncovered clues suggesting that inherited CDK12 mutations might be associated with ovarian cancer, although more research is needed to establish whether they increase the risk.

Several of the men with inherited CDK12 mutations had relatives with a history of ovarian cancer. The investigators also identified another person who had ovarian cancer and carried an inherited CDK12 mutation. Analysis of that person's tumor revealed the same characteristic genetic signature seen in the prostate cancer cases.

Together, these observations suggest that CDK12 could potentially play a role in hereditary cancer risk beyond the prostate. Further studies will be needed to determine how strongly the mutations are associated with ovarian cancer and whether they should influence screening recommendations.

For families carrying these rare mutations, the potential benefits of identifying their genetic risk could be substantial. Earlier testing may give relatives the opportunity to receive closer surveillance and, if cancer develops, begin treatment before it reaches an advanced stage.

"With the right genetic testing and screening programs, we envision a future where no one who inherits one of these mutations dies from cancer," said Dr. Wyatt.

The research received funding from the Prostate Cancer Foundation, Terry Fox Research Institute, Canadian Cancer Society, Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Michael Smith Health Research BC, U.S. National Institutes of Health, BC Cancer Foundation, and other funding partners.

#4343. How much does charging an EV really cost? This Redditor says $7 per month

One of the most common questions asked by first-time EV buyers is about the cost of electricity. Whether they plan to charge at home or find charging in the wild, everyone wants to know what to expect when it comes time to top off their batteries. One EV owner did the math after two months of EV ownership and came up with a surprising number: $7 a month.

Whether we’re talking gasoline, diesel, or electricity, one driver’s fuel costs can look dramatically different from another’s. How far they drive, how often, and under what conditions can matter just as much as what they drive. And while EVs may offer the greatest benefits to rural drivers covering long distances, a Redditor going by Suitable-Truth-350 took a different approach, moving into a highly walkable city for the express purpose of driving as little as possible.

“My wife and I recently retired and moved from a car dependent, rural/suburban area to a large, walkable city with good light rail. Our goal was to drive as little as possible,” write Suitable-Truth-350. “We took delivery of an Ioniq5 in August. We still have a daily walking life, but we use the car to see friends in the country, shop or travel around the greater Chicagoland area. After 2 months, we finally charged it.”

The result? Suitable says it took less than 30 minutes to juice their Ioniq 5 back up to an 80% SOC, at a total cost of $13.

“Driving the car is a pleasure,” they continue. “The pickup and smooth operation so different from our last ICE vehicle. First impression, we love the car and could never imagine going back to (a gasoline-powered car).”

I’ve been saying it for years: drive an EV for a week and whatever range anxiety you might experience will disappear. And, while it seems like Suitable-Truth-350 didn’t have much range anxiety to begin with, it’s worth noting here that their situation isn’t that rare.

In their most recent national survey, AAA found that the average US driver covered less than 29 miles per day, with the vast majority weekly commuting totals falling well within the range of even the most affordable used EVs.

The same survey found that just 30% of Americans reported taking at least one road trip the previous summer, with an average one-way trip length of ~235 miles.

That 235 mile trip might be too much for a car like the Fiat 500e, but even that car – the new EV with the shortest EPA-estimated range you can buy in the US – can make a 235 mile trip with a single 30-minute stop to charge. And in 2026 and 2027, they’re sure to find plenty of places to charge, thanks to a public charging network that’s newer, faster, and far more built out than they probably think, with more fast-charging locations opening every week and modern charging speeds that make longer stops the exception instead of the norm.

"That Redditor" is either full of it or drives only to the doctor's and back. In California, I spend just under $100 per month for my 28 mile 5 day/week commute in my Rivian R1T while keeping my speed between 55 and 60mph a vast majority of the time. My Tesla model 3 is about $63 for the same commute. My commute is, statistically, shorter than the average person in California.

In other words: your charging costs are probably going to be higher than Suitable-Truth-350’s seven-ish dollars per month, but with $4/gallon premium and $6/gallon diesel still very much the norm in 2026, it’ll probably be less than you think, too.

#4342. The Honda Avancier SUV Hints at the Next-Generation Hybrid CR-V

The Avancier is a three-row SUV that won’t be sold in the U.S. market, but it gives us an idea of what to expect with Honda’s upcoming hybrid product blitz.

Honda has revealed the second-generation Avancier today, and while it won’t be offered in the United States, the new SUV gives us a preview of the upcoming next-generation CR-V and other hybrid models due out over the next few years. Designed for Asian markets such as Thailand, Japan, and China, the three-row Avancier sits above the CR-V and pairs clean, modern styling with a new hybrid powertrain.

The Avancier debuts Honda’s new two-motor hybrid powertrain, called Honda Hybrid. For now, Honda is remaining tight-lipped about many of the details. The automaker promises “excellent fuel economy,” and the Avancier also launches Honda’s new DualPower eAWD system, controlling the front and rear wheels independently via separate electric motors. The S+ Shift function, which simulates gearshifts for the hybrid powertrain and has been seen on the Civic Hybrid and Prelude, is also present.

See all results for used Honda for sale near 20147

The Avancier is also the first Honda that is not an EV to feature the brand’s latest “H” logo, which was introduced in 2024 and was originally set to be used exclusively for electric models. With Honda cancelling its trio of EVs that were meant to be built in Ohio—the Acura RSX and Honda 0-Series Saloon and 0-Series SUV—the company has decided to roll out the simplified “H” logo across its entire lineup starting in 2027.

The new badge sits proudly on the nose of the Avancier, just below a thin opening that connects the squinting LED daytime running lights. The main headlights sit below, linked by a series of geometric trim pieces that, along with a vent in the lower bumper, help channel air to the engine.

The side profile of the Avancier is clean, with flush door handles and gloss black trim that frames the wheel arches and the bottom of the SUV. Around back, the taillights consist of blocky, vertical elements connected by a light bar. While we don’t think the next CR-V will look exactly like the Avancier, we expect to see elements such as the thin DRLs to migrate across the Honda lineup in the coming years.

The cabin will also likely inform future U.S.-bound Hondas, and it gives off an airy, tranquil vibe. Unfortunately, the Avancier appears to have skipped out on most physical controls, putting nearly every function into the sizable screen that sits above the air vents in the center of the dashboard. We hope Honda reconsiders this approach in the U.S., given how much we appreciate the intuitive, straightforward physical buttons and knobs found in current Hondas.

See all results for used Honda for sale near 20147

The Avancier also introduces a column-mounted shifter, a feature we also tested on a next-generation Civic prototype we drove last year. It frees up space on the center console. The steering wheel has an unusual squared-off shape with a flat bottom, and behind it there is a digital gauge cluster. Glowing ambient lighting and white upholstery create a futuristic, sterile appearance, and a panoramic glass roof extends all the way to the third row.

Honda loaded the SUV with premium features, such as heated and ventilated seats in the second row and a 12-speaker Bose stereo with Dolby Atmos. There’s also a system that uses cameras on the inside and outside of the Avancier to let owners check on the cabin and car’s surroundings remotely via a smartphone app.

While the Avancier won’t be sold on our shores, we expect to see elements of its styling on upcoming Hondas, as well as its new hybrid powertrain. Honda plans to launch 15 new hybrid models globally by 2030, which includes a new CR-V next year, as well as a new Civic and a heavily updated Accord in the near future.

#4341. NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound

NASA is pushing the limits of helicopter flight on Mars, testing rotor blades at speeds once considered too risky. The faster these blades spin, the more lift they can generate, potentially allowing future aircraft to carry heavier scientific instruments and travel greater distances across the Red Planet.

During tests conducted in March at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, engineers successfully pushed the tips of experimental Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound without causing them to break apart. The experiments took place inside a specialized chamber designed to reproduce the harsh atmospheric conditions on Mars. Results from 137 test runs could help engineers develop a new generation of more powerful aircraft capable of carrying scientific equipment.

"NASA had a great run with the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, but we are asking these next-generation aircraft to do even more at the Red Planet," said Al Chen, Mars Exploration Program manager at JPL. "That's not an easy ask. While everything about Mars is hard, flying there is just about the hardest thing you can do. That's because its atmosphere is so incredibly thin that it is hard to generate lift, and yet Mars has significant gravity."

Ingenuity made history on April 19, 2021, when it became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another world. However, it was designed primarily to demonstrate that flight on Mars was possible, not to transport scientific instruments. NASA now hopes to go much further. Its recently announced SkyFall project, along with other potential future aircraft, could carry sensors and scientific instruments to investigate Mars from the air. Flying at low altitudes would provide valuable information to support future robotic and human missions.

Why Flying on Mars Requires Extreme Rotor Speeds

Helicopters generate more thrust by spinning their rotors faster or using blades with a larger diameter. That basic principle applies on Earth and Mars, but the Red Planet presents a much greater engineering challenge.

Mars has an atmosphere only about 1% as dense as Earth's, leaving helicopter blades with far fewer air molecules to push against. To produce enough lift, engineers must operate rotors at exceptionally high speeds, bringing their tips close to the speed of sound. Small rotors on Earth can also spin thousands of times per minute, but the denser atmosphere makes it unnecessary to push their tips toward supersonic speeds to generate substantial lift.

During Ingenuity's 72 flights on Mars, its engineers limited the helicopter's composite-skinned foam rotors to 2,700 revolutions per minute. This restriction served two important purposes. It kept the blades away from the complex and potentially unpredictable conditions near the sound barrier, and it provided a safety margin in case sudden winds (from a dust devil, for instance) caused the blade tips to move faster relative to the surrounding air.

"If Chuck Yeager were here, he'd tell you things can get squirrely around Mach 1," said JPL's Jaakko Karras, the rotor test lead. "With that in mind, we planned Ingenuity's flights to keep the rotor blade tips at Mach 0.7 with no wind so that if we encountered a Martian headwind while in flight, the rotor tips wouldn't go supersonic. But we want more performance from our next-gen Mars aircraft. We needed to know that our rotors could go faster safely."

The speed of sound also differs considerably between the two planets. At sea level on Earth, Mach 1 is approximately 760 mph (1,223 kph). On Mars, sound travels at roughly 540 mph (869 kph), largely because the atmosphere is much colder and consists primarily of carbon dioxide.

NASA Tests Supersonic Rotors in a Mars Simulation Chamber

To determine whether the new blades could safely reach these extreme speeds, Karras and his colleagues used JPL's historic 25-Foot Space Simulator. The rotor systems were developed and manufactured by AeroVironment in Simi Valley, California.

The researchers began with a three-bladed rotor designed for potential future Mars helicopters. After installing it inside the chamber, they removed the surrounding air and introduced a carefully controlled amount of carbon dioxide to recreate the thin Martian atmosphere. They then spun the rotor at progressively higher speeds while exposing it to simulated winds.

Because the experiment involved the possibility of a rotor breaking apart at supersonic speeds, engineers reinforced part of the chamber with sheet metal. The team monitored the experiment from a control room located just a few yards away, using instruments and a camera to track the rotor's performance.

The rotor eventually reached 3,750 revolutions per minute, bringing its blade tips to Mach 0.98, just below the speed of sound. Engineers then switched on a fan to produce headwinds against the spinning blades. With each successive test, they increased the wind speed to push the system further.

Breaking the Sound Barrier Boosts Lift by 30%

The experiments ultimately drove the rotor tips to Mach 1.08, surpassing the sound barrier and increasing the aircraft's lift capability by 30%. Crucially, the blades survived the supersonic conditions.

That additional lift could make a major difference for future missions. More powerful Mars helicopters could transport heavier scientific instruments, advanced sensors, and larger batteries, allowing them to conduct more ambitious investigations and remain airborne for longer periods.

Following the successful tests of the three-bladed design, the team evaluated a second rotor intended for SkyFall. This version has two blades that are slightly longer than those used in the first configuration. Because of their greater length, the blade tips could reach the same near-supersonic speed at a lower rotational rate of 3,570 revolutions per minute before simulated headwinds were introduced.

"The successful testing of these rotors was a major step toward proving the feasibility of flight in more demanding environments, which is key for next-gen vehicles," said Shannah Withrow-Maser, an aerodynamicist from NASA's Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley and member of the test team. "We thought we'd be lucky to hit Mach 1.05, and we reached Mach 1.08 on our last runs. We're still digging into the data, and there may be even more thrust on the table. These next-gen helicopters are going to be amazing."

Next-Generation Mars Helicopters Could Launch in 2028

Engineers working on SkyFall have already incorporated the new test results into the project's performance specifications. The findings provide an important foundation for designing helicopters that can operate under more demanding conditions while carrying substantially more equipment than Ingenuity.

Inspired by the historic success of Ingenuity, which remains the only rotorcraft ever to fly on another planet, SkyFall is designed to transport three next-generation helicopters to Mars in December 2028.

If successfully developed and deployed, these aircraft could expand the possibilities for exploring Mars, providing scientists with a new way to investigate the planet's surface and gather information from locations that may be difficult for traditional rovers to reach.

#4340. The highly-anticipated follow-up to Baldur's Gate 3 is more Divinity, but it's not technically Original Sin 3

Larian has returned to tease a grand vision for its next major project, a new Divinity.

Larian Studios has delivered what was arguably the biggest reveal of The Game Awards 2025 showcase. The Hellstone, the mysterious monolith in the desert that’s been generating a lot of speculation in the lead-up to the show was indeed teasing the studio’s next game.

The Belgian developer is returning to the series it created with Divinity, a non-numbered sequel that’s designed for new and veteran players alike. The announcement was entirely cinematic, setting the tone for what looks to be the next big thing in the space.

Larian calls Divinity its most ambitious title ever, with the studio striving for a level of depth and breadth we’ve not seen before. This is the next project from the Baldur’s Gate 3 team, after all, so there’s understandably immense anticipation for it.

Divinity is a standalone RPG, and does not require you to have played Divinity: Original Sin, or Divinity: Original Sin 2. If you did, however, you’re going to find the journey extra special because of the continuity it offers.

“We’re ready to bring everything we’ve done previously into one place,” said founder and game director, Swen Vincke.

“This marks the beginning of something with more breadth, depth, and intimacy than anything we’ve created before. We’ve been building toward this moment ever since we took our fate into our own hands. This is the Divinity we’ve always wanted to make and you're going to have loads of fun with it.”

Beyond that, there’s precious little that’s been revealed for Divinity so far. We don’t know what platforms it’s going to be coming to, nor do we even have a release target. We do know it’s an RPG, so you can very much expect something similar to earlier games in the series, and, of course, Baldur’s Gate 3.

#4339. Tesla launches FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes

Tesla has started rolling out “Full Self-Driving” v15, and its list of improvements reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses: sign detection, potholes, and speed handling in school zones.

Tesla also claims “25x better handling of safety critical cases” and is adding a new live visualization that looks seriously impressive. If the driving improvements are as real as the visuals, this is a big update.

Tesla announced the rollout on X this afternoon, and its Tesla Super Intelligence account followed up with the full release notes. The company didn’t say which vehicles get it first, but it has previously told investors that its AI4 (HW4) computer is enough to run v15.

Here are Tesla’s release notes for FSD v15:

v15 upgrades every part of the end-to-end driving network. Includes:

Tesla’s main announcement also says FSD can now slow down for speed cameras, and it adds Bike Rack Mode, which allows FSD with a bike rack or a similar hitch accessory. Navigation learning only covers the start and end of trips for now; Tesla says later v15 releases will expand it to the entire route.

The new visualization is the flashiest part, and based on the video Tesla shared, it’s super impressive. The center screen shows a detailed, rendered version of the street around the car, far beyond the current FSD visualization.

FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network Safety25x better handling of safety critical casesTesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to doNavigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW

Tesla calls it “Reality View” in its announcement and “Tesla Augmented Reality” in the release notes. The notes say it replaces all the separate model signals with a single end-to-end visualization that uses less compute, and Tesla says it lets the driver “see & control what FSD is planning to do.” If that works as advertised, it could make supervising the system a lot easier.

What stands out more is where Tesla is focusing. Almost every driving improvement in the release notes targets an area where FSD struggles today.

Signs are a big one. In a test published in September, Brussels nonprofit Johanna.be found that FSD exceeded the limit in 55% of the 30 km/h zones it drove through, averaging 44 km/h. In most of those zones, the car’s screen showed a 50 km/h limit. It didn’t read the sign.

Potholes are another. In August, Musk said pothole avoidance was “coming soon”, something he had already promised back in 2019. Today, FSD still drives straight through them.

School zones are on the list too. NHTSA is reviewing a petition claiming Tesla’s Robotaxis speed through active school zones, on top of an investigation it opened in October 2025 into FSD traffic-law violations like running red lights. Slowing for speed cameras fits the same theme, though it also suggests Tesla is fine with FSD going over the limit when there’s no camera around.

So if v15 really fixes these, it’s a very good update. The question is by how much.

One change goes the other way. Tesla says it is “decreasing strictness” of driver monitoring in higher-speed driver profiles, at a time when sleeping drivers on FSD keep making headlines and Tesla is tightening monitoring in Europe at regulators’ request.

The release notes clear up what the “25x” refers to: Tesla says the new vision encoder improves the critical intervention rate by 25x. That’s the right metric to measure progress toward unsupervised driving. But Tesla still doesn’t share the actual number, only the multiplier.

The math gets interesting fast. Our data from earlier this year suggested FSD v14 could go a couple thousand miles between critical interventions. A 25x improvement on that would put v15 around 50,000 miles between critical interventions, well beyond the roughly 10,000 miles we’ve said Tesla needs for a limited unsupervised service. If that were true across the fleet, we could see Tesla having its most meaningful push toward autonomy in a long time.

And v15 already carries plenty of hype. In April, Elon Musk wrote that v15 “will far exceed human levels of safety, even in completely unsupervised and complex situations.” We pointed out at the time that he had said similar things about v12 and v14. In August, Tesla told JPMorgan that v15 is a “step-change” built on seven “core technologies,” with about 40% of them already running in its Robotaxi fleet in Austin.

FSD has never improved in a straight line. Every major version has brought real gains along with new problems, and point releases regularly go backward.

When v14 arrived in October 2025, it came with hallucinations, brake stabbing, and excessive speeding, and early crowdsourced data showed about 732 miles between critical disengagements, below what we expected. It then improved a lot. Then the v14.2 updates went backward before Musk sold v14.3 as the version where “the last big piece of the puzzle finally lands.”

Seven months and a long string of point releases later, owners are still supervising, and Tesla now needs v15 to deliver what v14.3 was supposed to.

I remain skeptic of Tesla's autonomous driving until they apply for the California DMV permit to begin testing autonomous driving without a driver. California is a big enough of a potential market for robotaxi that Tesla is operating a human driver taxi service. The common presumption is that Tesla is avoiding California autonomous testing because it requires disclosing critical interventions and other data which wouldn't be favorable to Tesla's claims.

The visuals are super impressive. That much we can already judge from the video, and Reality View could make FSD easier to understand and supervise.

The driving side is harder to judge. Tesla is going straight at the weaknesses that owners and regulators complain about most: misread speed limits, potholes, school zones, debris. If v15 delivers real progress on all of those, it’s a really good update.

But “improved detection” doesn’t tell us how much better, and a 25x multiplier without the underlying number is hard to check. FSD has gone two steps forward, one step back throughout its history, with point releases regularly breaking things the previous version handled fine. And Tesla still won’t publish the disengagement data that would settle it.

#4337. Arc Raiders' Cold Snap update brings snow storms to most maps, new events and a new Raider Deck

Arc Raiders has delivered a big new update that's very fittingly on theme, and it's not without new mechanics.

Arc Raiders is kicking off its last major event of the year. The Cold Snap update arrives moments from now, and it’s perhaps the game’s biggest since its momentous launch in late October. We’ve known about the existence of Cold Snap for a while, of course, but we finally have a solid idea about what to expect.

Cold Snap is made up of different components - including new content - that all players have access to.

As the name suggests, of course, Cold Snap introduces the new snowfall Map Condition. As part of this, maps will be covered in snow, thanks to snowstorms sweeping across them. For one, snowfall makes it harder to see enemies, but it also turns all lakes solid.

There’s a new mechanic associated with this, and it’s actually similar to Battlefield 6’s Winter Offensive update. Staying outdoors for too long will cause you to catch frostbite, which slowly drains HP. Embark says you’re going to need to bring more healing items with you on raids, and it doesn’t look like there are firepits that could keep you warm - though staying indoors for a while will help.

Cold Snap arrives alongside limited-time events that will be available until Tuesday, January 13. The snowfall visual update and new frostbite mechanics are available on Dam Battlegrounds, Buried City, Spaceport, and The Blue Gate.

One of the new events is Flickering Flames, which comes with its own progression track of 25 levels. Content is, of course, unlocked using Merits, which are earned from XP in matches. The other event is the Candleberry Banquet Project, which requires you to donate items found on the surface (including Candleberries).

You’ll earn rewards each time, and each stage completed will reveal a new scene on the banquet table. Likewise, there are cosmetic rewards as part of each stage, and you can use it as a source of Merits, too.

While on the subject, the new update also kicks off a new Raider Deck (battle pass). Available from December 26, The Goalie Raider Deck is pretty much what you’d expect. You’ll find several pages of cosmetic and useful items. The new Deck will be available to all players for free.

#4336. Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist

As temperatures rise, the floating ice shelves that help hold Antarctica's massive ice sheet in place are melting and breaking apart at record rates. As these protective barriers disappear, they expose towering walls of solid ice. Whether these cliffs remain standing or collapse could play a major role in Antarctica's future ice loss and its contribution to rising sea levels worldwide.

For years, scientists have believed that ice cliffs become unstable once they exceed 100 meters in height, roughly as tall as the Statue of Liberty. According to this theory, a cliff that grows too tall will collapse under its own weight, exposing an even taller wall of ice farther inland. That new cliff would then collapse, potentially setting off a chain reaction that causes the ice sheet to retreat rapidly.

But new research from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) challenges this long-standing assumption. The findings suggest that the fate of an Antarctic ice cliff depends on much more than its height, and that even dramatic collapses do not necessarily lead to an unstoppable retreat.

Published in the journal Science, the study examined satellite observations of more than 15,000 Antarctic ice cliffs collected over four years. Researchers discovered a surprising pattern: When the cliffs collapsed, they sometimes retreated much faster than existing models predicted. Yet rather than continuing to disintegrate, the affected glaciers soon stabilized.

"We found that when the cliffs were retreating, they were doing so faster than what has been modeled, which would mean more ice loss and higher contributions of sea level rise," says study author Caroline Needell, a graduate student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program. "But because we found that the retreat was short-lived, and all the glaciers eventually stabilized, that would suggest that things won't be so bad. We don't see this runaway effect."

The study's co-authors are Catherine Walker, an assistant scientist at WHOI, and Jeremy Bassis, an associate professor at the University of Michigan.

Why Scientists Expected Antarctica's Ice Cliffs to Collapse

The possibility of runaway ice cliff collapse is described by a theory called marine ice cliff instability (MICI). It proposes that when an exposed ice wall reaches a critical height, its own weight makes it structurally unstable. If the cliff falls and reveals an even taller wall behind it, the process could repeat, progressively eating away at the Antarctic ice sheet.

Earlier research investigated this possibility primarily through computer models. Scientists used the physical properties of ice to estimate how enormous frozen cliffs should behave, then compared those calculations with a limited number of observations from Antarctica. These studies suggested that cliffs taller than approximately 100 meters were particularly vulnerable to collapse.

"Predictive ice-sheet models that have been used so far to represent ice cliff instability just take into account cliff height," Needell notes. "That's the only variable that matters. And once the cliff height reaches the critical threshold, usually 100 meters, it should initiate this runaway effect of ice sheet retreat."

Needell and her colleagues wanted to test those predictions against a much larger collection of real-world measurements. They sought to determine how tall Antarctica's ice cliffs actually become and whether their collapse consistently triggers the destructive chain reactions predicted by existing models.

Satellites Reveal Surprising Ice Cliff Stability

To investigate, the researchers turned to NASA's Ice, Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2). This spacecraft repeatedly travels over Earth's polar regions, using a laser-based instrument called an altimeter to measure elevations with great precision. Its observations track the heights of glaciers, ice sheets, and sea ice, as well as ocean levels in and around Antarctica.

The team analyzed measurements gathered between 2019 and 2023, examining more than 15,000 ice cliffs at three-month intervals. Most were far shorter than the height considered dangerous by earlier models. The average cliff stood approximately 30 meters tall, although a small number exceeded the proposed 100-meter instability threshold.

The researchers also searched for characteristics that might explain why some cliffs remained stable while others retreated.

One important clue came from the broken ice accumulating in front of the cliffs. Known as mélange, this material consists of a slushy mixture of sea ice and fragments of icebergs. Cliffs that remained relatively stationary tended to have thicker accumulations of mélange, suggesting that the debris could help support the towering ice walls.

"We measured mélange height and found taller cliffs have thicker mélange, which could be a built-in stabilizing effect," Needell explains.

Surrounding seawater provided another possible source of stability. The observations indicated that deeper water can exert greater supporting pressure against an ice cliff, helping counteract the forces that might otherwise cause it to collapse.

Together, these findings suggest that the stability of Antarctica's ice cliffs cannot be predicted by height alone. Conditions in the water surrounding the ice may also determine whether a cliff remains standing.

Antarctica's Tallest Ice Cliffs Collapse, Then Stabilize

"After we did that global analysis, we thought, ok, let's zoom in on the tallest cliffs and see how they're behaving," Needell says.

The researchers selected four locations around Antarctica where satellites had recorded some of the tallest ice cliffs. Each stood approximately 100 meters high, with the tallest reaching 127 meters. The team then reconstructed how these cliffs changed at three-month intervals throughout the four-year study.

The results initially appeared to support the idea that extremely tall cliffs are unstable. These towering walls did collapse, and the glaciers behind them retreated at speeds substantially greater than those anticipated by existing MICI models.

However, the retreat did not continue indefinitely.

"But that retreat was short-lived," Needell notes.

Instead of retreating farther inland in a continuous series of collapses, the glaciers stabilized and eventually advanced outward toward the ocean again.

"It's this rapid retreat, punctuated by periods of stabilization," Needell says. "That was puzzling to us. Then, we thought: We need to look at all the things that affect cliff height."

The unexpected pattern suggested that some overlooked physical processes were interrupting the collapse before it could develop into a sustained chain reaction.

Hidden Ridges Beneath the Ice Act as Natural Speed Bumps

To understand what was stopping the retreat, the team examined the shape of the land beneath Antarctica's ice sheet.

This underlying terrain, known as bed topography, can strongly influence the height and stability of the ice above it. When the ground is relatively flat, the visible slope of the ice more closely reflects the thickness of the ice itself. But when the terrain rises into a ridge or bump, the ice resting on that elevated ground is thinner than its overall surface elevation might suggest.

These buried rises can function like natural speed bumps. By reducing the thickness of the overlying ice, they can make exposed cliffs shorter and less vulnerable to collapse.

When the scientists compared the locations of stabilizing ice cliffs with measurements of Antarctica's underlying terrain, they found that the cliffs frequently stopped retreating where the ground rose beneath them.

The researchers identified another important process. Taller cliffs tended to "thin out" more rapidly as they collapsed. Rather than remaining towering, unstable walls, they could quickly shrink into shorter cliffs that were better able to withstand further collapse.

These effects help explain why the researchers observed rapid initial ice loss followed by periods of stability, rather than the continuous retreat anticipated by earlier models.

What the Discovery Means for Future Sea Level Rise

The findings could help scientists improve predictions of how Antarctica's ice sheet will respond to continued warming.

Although the researchers observed some cliffs collapsing faster than expected, the rapid retreat was temporary in the locations they studied. This challenges the assumption that crossing a particular height threshold inevitably leads to runaway collapse.

The results do not mean Antarctica's ice sheet is safe from further losses. Instead, they reveal that predicting its future requires accounting for several interacting factors, including the shape of the land beneath the ice, the rate at which ice becomes thinner, the depth of surrounding water, and the stabilizing effects of broken ice.

"Now we know what to look for," Needell says. "We really need to know the bed topography, and we need to know the ice thinning rate, in order to get ice cliff instability right, because this value really matters in the context of projecting sea level rise."

By incorporating these additional processes into ice sheet models, scientists may be able to produce more reliable estimates of Antarctica's future contribution to global sea level rise.

The research received partial support from NASA, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the DOMINOS project, which is part of the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration.

#4335. Here are 7 great reasons rural drivers SHOULD embrace EVs in 2027

America’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification. In fact, EVs offer rural drivers even more benefits than they do to city-dwellers!

UPDATE 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.

“An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura. “Rural communities across the country have their own distinguishing characteristics, but certain shared characteristics such as driving distances, the type of vehicles driven, and socio-economics are factors which contribute to this larger potential to benefit from vehicle electrification.”

Pinto de Moura went on to outline five ways rural and country drivers could benefit from going electric – but that was in 2021, and a whole lot has changed in the nearly six years since. As such, I thought it was high time we revisit some of the reasons EVs are a great fit for rural lifestyles, see if we could uncover any new ones, and outline the reasons we think rural drivers should rush to embrace electric vehicles in the coming calendar year.

When you hear that line about, “the average American drives 30 to 40 miles a day,” remember that in towns like Wellington, Ohio, or Colfax, Washington, 30 miles is a grocery run. Each way. So when people trot out that old line about range anxiety, what rural drivers actually hear isn’t reassurance. It’s dismissal — a suggestion that they drive too far for an EV to work, when nothing could be further from the truth.

A recent study by Rural Climate Partnership found that rural drivers spend an average of 44% more on fuel than city dwellers, and that the top 3.6% of rural drivers — the “supermilers” who rack up the most miles — could save over $4,000 each year by switching to electric fuel.

Country guys and gals love their pickups, and arguably the biggest difference between the EV market of 2021 and 2027 is that electric trucks and SUVs are no longer a novelty. There are now battery-powered options ready to haul, handle chores, head out camping, and tow a trailer.

What’s more, a new wave of more affordable electric trucks from Ford, Slate, and others is challenging the idea that you need a $50,000 half-ton pickup to get real work done. Early interest suggests there’s plenty of pent-up demand for capable, accessible electric work trucks that don’t need to be twenty feet long or cost more than what your parent’s paid for their house.

With only about 45% of rural counties having access to DC fast charging, public charging still isn’t as visible as many first-time EV buyers might like, but it’s far better than it used to be — and improving fast. Still, that’s not the real EV advantage. Home charging is.

Unlike many apartment-dwelling urban drivers, most rural owners can charge right at home. More than 80% of rural households have a driveway or garage that are ideal for overnight Level 2 charging, and many already have a 240V outlet, keeping setup costs (if there even are any) to a minimum.

Plug in before bed, wake up to a full battery every morning, and do it for pennies on the dollar, especially with off-peak rates.

If disaster strikes and you lose power, your EV could be more than just a way to get around. Many electric cars and trucks have the ability to power refrigerators, freezers, well pumps, lights, and other household essentials for days, either through onboard outlets or a dedicated vehicle-to-home (V2H) system that feeds electricity directly into your home’s electrical panel. Ford’s from-the-ashes F-150 Lightning and Tesla’s Cybertruck are already among the EVs making that capability a reality, and newer, more affordable electric trucks promise to bring V2H tech to even more households.

If you live in an area prone to extreme weather, where severe storms, hurricanes, or wildfires can leave homes without electricity for days, that’s a pretty compelling benefit. Keeping food cold, medical equipment running or essential medication refrigerated can be a literal lifesaver – and your EV’s battery might be the biggest backup power source you own.

It’s been a few years since a working class guy could reasonably expect to get a new pickup for less than $50,000. And, while much has been made of the “high cost of electric vehicles,” the truth is that thanks to killer lease deals, new tax incentives, and companies like Ford Pro and TRC that are willing to help you find even more funding to help pay for them, EVs can often be had for less than a comparable gas model.

As such, getting behind the wheel of an ultra-powerful, ultra smooth-running electric pickup truck from your favorite brand is easier than ever.

At the risk of sounding like a paranoid red hat, rural Americans are proud Americans – just like rural Canadians are proud Canadians. Unfortunately, every gallon of gas burned in their pickups and SUVs came from oil drilled, refined, and traded on global markets — and that means supporting the oil business and economies of nations whose values don’t always align with, or maybe are even outright hostile to theirs.

Switching to an EV can help more of that money right here at home, especially as more and better battery recycling efforts come online and newer battery and anode/cathode chemistries are developed, reducing dependence on rare Earth metals, cobalt, and even lithium.

Even better, thanks to the rapid expansion and dramatically reduced costs of wind and solar power, you can power your EV with energy that is 100% Made in the USA, that doesn’t support foreign oil interests or involve you in a bunch of dumb oil wars (except indirectly), and which creates good-paying construction and maintenance jobs for local workers.

In my experience, rural buyers appreciate things that last, and are moved more by lasting quality than fleeting fashions – and that’s exactly why they should be looking at EVs.

We recently covered a 2019 Chevy Bolt that had put more than 470,000 miles on its odometer, along with data from Ford showing its battery packs maintain more than 90% of their battery health after 100,000 miles.

And while we’re talking about data, it should be noted that EVs aren’t some new, unknown technology. The first modern high-voltage car battery hit the road more than 30 years ago (the Prius was released in 1996, as a 1997 model). Some of those cars are still on the road – and there are literally tens of thousands of EVs out there still performing their daily driver duties every day.

There are obviously more reasons to go electric than these, from lower cost of ownership to saving the planet to absolutely killer burnouts that would make the one-tire-fire era IROC Camaros hang their 305s in shame – but I think those kind of fade into the background as being appealing to just about everyone, instead of being especially appealing to rural drivers.

I live in rural Australia in a village that doesn't even have a fuel bowser. My shopping trip is usually around 164km (100miles). I have solar on my roof. I now have an EV (one of the Chinese brands that aren't available in the USA) and am delighted with it. I'm saving a lot of money on fuel and because the solar feed-in tariff goes negative in the middle of the day (I have to pay the utility company to take my electricity) by charging the car at home I save money there. For rural people with roof space for solar EVs should be a no-brainer, but like many rural areas my district is incredibly conservative (do a search for Barnaby Joyce, my local member) and the populace are convinced they don't drive far enough, they'll catch on fire (mine has an LFP battery, so the risk is low) and that I'll need to replace the battery in a year (even though the battery has an 8 year warranty).

That said, it’s been a long time since I was back in Ohio, so maybe I’ve forgotten what it’s like. You guys are smart, head on down to the comments and let me know what I missed!

#4334. Genesis Wants to Build and Sell the 1100-HP X Skorpio Desert Runner

And despite previous plans to limit the vehicle to wealthy customers in the Middle East, the luxury trophy truck could make its way Stateside.

Now that GTA VI has launched, something seems to have gotten into the minds of the executives over at Genesis. The company is actively working to bring the 1100-horsepower X Skorpio concept to production by 2030, Hyundai CEO Jose Muñoz said, according to an Automotive News report.

If you haven’t seen the X Skorpio before now, we’d forgive you for thinking it came straight out of the newest title from Rockstar Games. The batmobile-esque desert runner is built on a tubular frame with an integrated roll cage, and its bodywork is made of carbon fiber, Kevlar, and fiberglass. Oh, and it’s packing a dedicated race engine that produces 1100 horsepower, 850 pound-feet of torque, and a sound that will send all the dogs in your neighborhood scurrying for cover.

See all results for used Genesis for sale near 98382

Limited production of the X Skorpio was always all but guaranteed. Genesis told Car and Driver that the first orders for the X Skorpio arrived within minutes of the concept’s reveal.

That said, Muñoz’s latest comments directly contradict the brand’s messaging when it first showed the X Skorpio concept earlier this year. When we spoke with Luc Donckerwolke, the brand’s chief creative officer, at the reveal of the X Skorpio in January, he told us outright that there were no plans to bring it to the United States and that it would instead remain a toy for wealthy customers in the Middle East. Perhaps enough American customers with the money to purchase a trophy truck as a hobby have lobbied Genesis to bring the wild machine Stateside.

Those customers will need to be willing to put up with a few drawbacks, though, because even if a production version of the X Skorpio does make its way to Genesis showrooms in the U.S., its design will keep it from earning street-legal status.

Jack Fitzgerald’s love for cars stems from his as yet unshakable addiction to Formula 1. #4333. Arc Raiders' latest patch adds two of the most requested features, but kills Cred hoarding

The last major Arc Raiders update of the year has arrived, bringing several big new features to the game, but not without some bad news.

Embark has just rolled out patch 1.7.0 for Arc Raiders players everywhere. This is a significant patch for the extraction shooter for a number of reasons, not least of which because it kicks off a series of events under the Cold Snap banner, which introduces a new conditions to the game’s maps.

Dig deeper into the patch notes, however, and you’ll find even more to get excited about, including features players have been asking for since the game’s first public test.

To start with, today’s update finally adds an option toggle aiming down sights. This is especially relevant for PC players, most of whom play shooters with an ADS toggle, rather than hold. Another often requested feature has been the ability to reset the game’s skill tree.

This is now available for the cost of 2,000 Coins per skill point. It goes without saying that you’re going to need a whole lot of money to reset the entire thing, but it’s a useful option to have when you want to alter your path.

The next change is one that’s going to ruffle a lot of feathers. Arc Raiders now has a soft Cred cap of 800. This is now clearly shown on your Wallet screen, and the developer said the cap is necessary to prevent players from using their accumulated Cred to unlock new Raider Decks immediately after release.

The good news is that this won’t affect the Cred you may already have, but going forward, 800 is the most you can hold at any point. You’ll also notice that Shani has more stuff for you to buy with Cred, in case you want another way to spend what you have.

Patch 1.7.0 also brings a few other additions - and makes some changes - that are worth highlighting. You can now customise your Raider Tool, which likely means we’re going to see Raider Tool cosmetics going forward.

Speaking of items, the Aphelion weapon blueprint has been moved to Stella Montis, so you won’t be able to get it from taking down the Matriarch. The Bettina, and Rattler have both seen some balance changes.

The Bettina’s durability will now degrade a lot slower per shot, making it take 26 magazines to fully deplete durability. The base magazine size has been increased to 22, and the reload time has been cut to 4.5 seconds. Embark says this should make the weapon more viable in PvP, while also allowing it to stand on its own without the need for players bring a secondary weapon.

As for the Rattler, the only change it gets is an increase to its magazine size from 10 to 12. The idea is to make it about as effective as a Stitcher or Kettle at close ranges when it comes to PvP encounters.

And, of course, it wouldn’t be a big Arc Raiders patch without some tweaks to the game’s Arc enemies. This time, the Shredder gets all the love. The menacing unit now moves faster, turns more sharply and doesn’t get knocked back as much when shot.

The Shredder’s head now has more health, too, meaning you won’t be able to shoot it off early and confuse it. In general, the Arc unit should be smarter, especially when navigating narrow spaces. Finally, the Shredder now activates faster upon detecting (and being attacked by) players.

Beyond that, the main menu has seen a few changes to highlight ongoing events, make certain announcements quieter, make it easier to track Raider Quests and more. There’s a lot more in this update, too, such as changes to footstep loudness, several tweaks to loot and the value of certain items, and more besides. You’ll find the full change log on the official website.

#4332. Xiaomi’s 1,548 hp electric supercar is going global, starting in the UAE

As a red wave of Chinese-built electric vehicles breaks over Europe and Canada, Xiaomi is selling its electric cars outside of China for the first time ever – and its starting its push for global growth with the UAE in 2027.

Xiaomi is selling its electrified vehicles to buyers outside of China for first time this week, with the SU7 sedan, YU7 crossover, and Skynomad SUV now listed for sale throughout the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The company isn’t going it alone, however.

Xiomi is working local distributor Gargash Prime Automotive, rather than operating its own retail network, with Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun confirming that the company would officially enter Western car markets next year at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen held 17NOV.

CarNewsChina reports that Gargash Prime Automotive is offering 13 variants across the Xiaomi SU7 sedan, YU7 SUV, and Skynomad extended-range electric SUV lineup, with retail prices starting at 169,900 AED ($~46,200 US) for the SU7 Standard and climbing all the way up to 375,900 AED ($~102,000 US) for the range-topping SU7 Ultra.

Not to lump a bunch of nations with their own rich heritage and car culture together, but it’s fair to say that drivers in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait love their supercars – and the brand’s Xiaomi SU7 Ultra might be one of the most super of them all, thanks to fully 1,548 hp from three high-torque electric motors, the SU7 Ultra can sprint from 0-100 km/h (62 mph) in under two seconds on its way to a towering, 217 mph top speed.

It’s not just a straight-line speed machine, either. Xiaomi gave its go-fast flagship a serious track-focused makeover on its way to becomig the “Utlra,” complete with carbon-ceramic brakes, an aggressive (if controversial) composite aero package, an enormous rear wing, and a chassis tuned to tackle the turns the Green Hell of the Nürburgring.

And, at a relatively reasonable $102,000 equivalent price, I’d be willing to bet that a lot of the hypercar-loving Emiratis will be eager to get their hands on one.

The first customer deliveries of the Xiaomi SU7 Standard and Ultra, YU7 Standard, and Skynomad N70 Pro models are scheduled for December of this year, with deliveries of the remaining variants scheduled for February 2027.
