#4303. Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale Is the Purest Prancing Horse in Years

The 296 CS adds serious aero and ditches the GTB's hybrid system for a more enthusiast-focused driving experience.

Nostalgia must be in the air in Maranello. A few months ago, Ferrari unveiled the 12Cilindri Manuale, reintroducing a (simulated) six-speed manual transmission to its model lineup purely for the sake of driver involvement. And now, the Challenge Stradale badge returns to the rear engine mesh of a Prancing Horse for the first time since the 360 CS was discontinued in 2004. Simply put, it's a good year to be a sentimental Ferrarista.

In the same vein as its predecessor, the 296 Challenge Stradale is a road car that shares its fundamental philosophy with the new 296 Challenge Evo racecar, which will debut in the single-marque Ferrari Challenge racing series next year. Parked side by side at their reveal at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya today, we would excuse a gentleman driver for confusing the CS with his new track-only machinery.

See all results for Ferrari 296 for sale near 29405

There have been several limited-edition, track-focused mid-engine Ferraris since the 360 Challenge Stradale—including the F430 Scuderia, 458 Speciale, and 488 Pista—but the 296 Challenge Stradale goes the furthest of all of them in emulating its racecar counterpart, both aesthetically and mechanically.

While previous track-centric Ferraris have been somewhat demurely styled, the 296 CS puts its aerodynamic elements on full display. The carbon-fiber rear wing, dive planes, adjustable front splitter, and vented hood are essentially a copy-paste job from the Challenge Evo, with concessions made for road legality. Up front, twin vents positioned in the hood just before the windshield channel hot air expelled from two under-hood radiators over the windshield and towards the rear of the car, reducing the aerodynamic variations caused by changing ground clearance.

Other aero features are hidden out of sight. The CS's underbody has been smoothed to better feed the rear diffuser and work with three pairs of vortex generators at the front and two at the rear to generate additional downforce. With all of the aerodynamic elements colluding, the 296 Challenge Stradale makes 1360 pounds of downforce at 155 mph. That's a 72-percent increase over the base 296GTB's peak figure.

Big changes have been made to the CS's powertrain. You won't find any orange high-voltage wiring snaking around under the glass of its mid-mounted hood like you would in a 296GTB or 296 Speciale, as the 5-kWh battery pack and rear-mounted axial-flux electric motor have been removed entirely. The twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 operates unassisted and supposedly sounds better than ever courtesy of a reworked twin-exit exhaust system.

See all results for Ferrari 296 for sale near 29405

Overall firepower has decreased to 670 horsepower—149 ponies less than the standard 296GTB's. The upside is a notable decrease in mass, with Ferrari claiming that the removal of the plug-in-hybrid componentry played a major role in shedding 328 pounds from the 296GTB's dry weight. A lightened transmission flex plate, driveshaft, and timing cover were also developed to make the CS's powertrain as featherweight as possible. Without an electric motor present to fill in any thrust gaps left by turbo lag, the V-6 has been retuned to increase low-end grunt, although peak torque remains 546 pound-feet delivered at 8250 rpm.

As to be expected, yanking out an integrated powertrain system comes with some unique challenges that affect more than just the engine itself. For example, Ferrari was forced to enlarge the 296 CS's rear carbon-ceramic brake discs and the ventilation ducts that cool them to compensate for the lack of regenerative braking. The decreased weight in the rear also shifted its weight distribution 1.5 percent to the front, which was addressed with suspension design and geometry changes.

The CS's newly developed suspension is derived directly from the 296 Challenge Evo and features semi-active dampers and a dual-spring design that improves rebound response. The result is reduced body roll, which helps the performance of the specially developed Pirelli P Zero R tires, measuring 245/35R20 in the front and 305/35R20 in the rear. The 20-inch forged wheels can be ordered in Matte Grigio Corsa, Matte Nero with a diamond-cut finish, or Matte Bianco Fuji.

The 296 Challenge Stradale's cockpit is very similar to the one found in the 296 Speciale. While niceties like climate control and a stereo remain, carbon-fiber door panels and a lack of armrests and storage pockets are a clear indication of the CS's weight-saving mission. For true gluttons for punishment, an even further stripped interior spec is available that removes the trim from the area beneath the seats and the lower section of the carpets beneath the center console, leaving part of the chassis exposed.

Ferrari is adamant that the 296 CS isn't a replacement for the 296 Speciale and will not cannibalize that model's customer base, as the two are intended for different buyers. Besides being geared less towards outright track duty, the 296 Speciale is a part of Ferrari's special series, meaning that customers need to have an "existing relationship" with the brand in order to get an allocation. The 296 Challenge Stradale is a standard range model, meaning anyone can walk into a dealer and order one, existing relationship or not. Ferrari says that it wants to court new Ferrari buyers interested in experiencing the purest driving experience that the prancing horse has to offer, and the 296 CS is the first step in that direction.

U.S. pricing has not been announced, but in its home market, the 296 Challenge Stradale costs 291,000 euros, or the equivalent of about $320,000. Stateside deliveries of the new CS are expected to begin sometime in late 2027. As a non-Speciale model, CS production numbers aren’t limited, which presents a unique opportunity to buy a special new Ferrari without already owning one.

#4302. For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard

How often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout. A large study of Norwegian college students found that those who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety one year later. The findings suggest that maintaining a consistent exercise routine could be particularly important for supporting mental well-being.

The research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues. Their results point to the potential benefits of exercising regularly rather than focusing primarily on longer or more demanding workouts.

Why Exercise Habits Matter for Mental Health

Depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide. The college years can be an especially challenging period as students adjust to new academic, social, and personal responsibilities. Identifying everyday behaviors that may help protect mental health is therefore an important research priority.

Although previous research has linked regular physical activity to better psychological well-being, many young adults remain physically inactive. Scientists have also had relatively limited evidence about how exercise habits relate to the development of mental health conditions over time, particularly when those conditions are evaluated using standardized diagnostic tools.

To investigate this relationship, Grasdalsmoen and his team followed 10,460 full-time students enrolled in higher education in Norway. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 35.

At the beginning of the study, students completed questionnaires describing their exercise habits, including how frequently they worked out, how strenuous their activities were, how long they exercised, and how many total hours they were active each week. One year later, they completed a self-administered diagnostic assessment designed to identify common mental health disorders.

Exercise Frequency May Matter More Than Intensity

The researchers found that students who reported lower levels of physical activity were more likely to meet diagnostic criteria for anxiety or depression one year later. However, not every aspect of exercise showed the same relationship with mental health.

Exercise frequency emerged as a particularly consistent factor. How often students exercised was more reliably associated with their later mental health than the intensity of their workouts or the amount of time they spent exercising.

The researchers also identified differences between men and women. Among women, lower exercise intensity was associated with a greater likelihood of anxiety and depression. Among men, spending fewer total hours exercising each week showed a stronger association with these conditions.

Overall, the likelihood of common mental health disorders decreased as weekly exercise increased, with this pattern continuing up to approximately 10 hours of physical activity per week.

The results also support the World Health Organization's recommendation that adults complete at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week.

Regular Exercise Could Help Support Student Mental Health

Taken together, the findings suggest that exercising consistently may be especially valuable for reducing the likelihood of anxiety and depression among college students. Rather than concentrating exclusively on workout intensity or duration, maintaining a regular routine could be an important part of supporting mental health.

However, the researchers emphasize that their observational study cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Although students who exercised more regularly tended to have better mental health outcomes, the results do not prove that exercise itself prevented depression or anxiety.

Even with this limitation, promoting accessible opportunities for physical activity could be a useful part of broader efforts to improve student well-being. Such efforts may be especially relevant for students who are beginning to experience mental health difficulties or symptoms that have not yet reached the threshold for a clinical diagnosis.

The authors add: "Our findings show that students who engage in regular physical exercise are at lower risk of developing common mental disorders over time. These findings highlight the importance of making physical activity an accessible and natural part of student life."

"Mental health among students is a growing public health concern. Our findings suggest that supporting students to be physically active may contribute to better mental health and should be recognized as an important part of a healthy learning environment."

Funding: The SHoT study was financially supported by the Norwegian Ministry of Education and Research (2017) and the Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services (2016). Neither funding organization participated in designing the research, collecting or analyzing data, deciding whether to publish the findings, or preparing the manuscript.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

#4299. Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," says Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone."

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss

Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating plans, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several important indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes

The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

These differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially important distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits."

Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

#4298. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

Each game has its own real physical play pieces that interact with the action onscreen, often in innovative and charming ways. Think of it as the best of both worlds between board games and video games, and you’ll get what they’re shooting for here. $399

Few additions to the latest Dungeons & Dragons rules pack as much punch and value as this new expansion, focusing on ways to develop further and evolve the use of magic across your tabletop gaming sessions. New subclasses, spells, creatures, magical items, and factions add thoughtful, intriguing options for both players looking to play someone new and DMs hunting for new story hooks and challenges. $50

If you’re as excited as we are about this month’s celebration of the Tomb Raider legacy (see p. 40), this centerpiece statue is an ideal fit for your collection. Standing roughly nine inches in height, Lara is poised for exploration in her original classic garb. The sculpt strikes a perfect balance between crisp detail and stylistic presentation, in line with that early version of the character; the metallic blue motorcycle paint is especially striking. $250

For players longing for the glory days of stand-up arcade games, it’s hard to beat Arcade 1Up’s approach. The team’s sturdy cabinets look and sound great as a marquee feature of your game room. The new Outrun machine features much of the original display art, a bright 19-inch screen, and responsive gas and brake pedals as you steer around those tight corners. Sega has packed in OutRun, Turbo OutRun, OutRunners, and Power Drift. If old-school racing isn’t your thing, look for cabinets that run the gamut from Pac-Man to Joust to Claw Machines. $629.99

The long-running Nendoroid figures continue to be an attractive but still affordable choice for building collections across numerous fan-favorite series. There are somewhere around 2000 characters at this point! New entries like the Genshin Impact collection make a strong case for the line. The look is chibi, the quality is excellent, poseability is high, and customizable face and accessory parts let you change up your display over time. $46

We’ve previously sung the praises of Libernovo’s versatile approach to an ergonomic gaming chair, which includes a lumbar stretch functionality, a steady recline option for comfortable pushback without sudden shifts, and dynamically adjusting parts as you move through your day. The Maxis line does all that, but addresses one of the fundamental problems for at least some users with the original – it wasn’t big enough. With features like a wider base and longer headrest reach, the Maxis aims to provide the same comfort to the players who are tall or wide enough to need the extra breathing room. $1119

If you’re the player on your team who likes to have easy access to soundboards and real-time voice changing, the Key Pocket could be just the ticket. This small device straps onto your phone for mobile play, but it’s also compatible with consoles, Discord, Twitch, or just about any place you want to tweak audio on the fly. A free tier gives you access to some voice-changing and sounds, while a separate subscription opens up hundreds of thousands of additional options. But be warned: we can’t help you after your friends abandon you for that baby voice you won’t stop using. $99

The question of the best bang for your buck in modern consoles has become extraordinarily complicated, especially as tech prices have soared in recent years. There’s no right answer, but Sony’s high-end machine walks the line of offering extremely high-tier performance without escalating to even higher-priced gaming PCs. Higher and more consistent frame rates than on standard PS5, advanced ray tracing, and an increasing number of games that feature enhanced PSSR image options all add up to a better gaming experience, if you’re ready to make the significant price jump. $900

If the gamer in your life is looking for a stylish, understated way to express their love of the hobby, Anicorn’s designer watch collaboration with PlayStation could be a standout option. Available in black and a slick silver/white combo, the minimalist timepiece includes the familiar face buttons of Sony’s controller encased in an oil-injection display so they slowly and freely float across the watch as you move. $250

It’s a safe bet you’ve at least seen the popular Shashibo puzzle cubes by this point. We’ve been fans of their brain-teasing, fidgety fun for some time. Battle Shapes takes the core concept – reshaping the box into various distinct magnetically-locked shapes – and extends it into a timed game experience, playable solo or head-to-head. By targeting specific shapes, you significantly improve your speed with the toy, and scannable QR codes on the cards offer clear tutorials for each shape so you can prep for competition. $50

While the vast majority of gamers looking for good personal audio are going to be okay with a larger set of cans over their ears, We know more than a few players for whom that’s a definite no – for comfort, awareness of surrounding sounds, or other reasons. The Arc 5 earbuds aim to solve for that, with an over-ear design that feels extremely comfortable. And because they sit on the ear, you can still hear what’s going on around you. While that limits some aspects of the final sound quality, the inclusion of THX certification, Dolby Atmos optimization, and Dynamic Bass Enhancement helps to ensure audio is still very strong. $230

Across Lego’s many recent themes, Tolkien’s legendarium has offered some stellar sets. The largest yet is the capital of Gondor, with an astonishing 8,278 pieces and a height of roughly two feet. The castle/city build is impressive, featuring tons of interesting angles and turns. The finished product aims to offer the best of both worlds in presentation – a microscale representation of the front façade and a reverse minifigure-scale Hall of Kings. We especially like the inclusion of Denethor’s cherry tomatoes. $650

The original Azul is often cited as a foundational entry in modern board gaming. The “Kids” versions of celebrated titles aren’t always a sure bet, but this one holds up to scrutiny. Azul Kids lowers the complexity threshold but keeps the foundational strategic thinking. Players lay out uniquely shaped tiles into mosaic frameworks in colorful, appealing patterns; the basic concept of the original inspiration is clear, and kids as young as five can grasp and enjoy the fun. $25

Many corners of the collecting world have embraced the fun (and frequent despair) of blind boxes, where you never know exactly who you’ll get in a given series. Funism has a strong track record for quality, offering adorable smaller figures like their latest line of Evangelion collectibles. Each figure stands nearly four inches and features both human characters and mecha. You can buy singles and roll the dice, or purchase larger sets with a no-duplicates guarantee, which can save a lot of heartache if you’re trying to line your whole shelf. $21

If you’re going to spring for a high-end keyboard for PC gaming, it’s important that you like the feel of the keys. The slightly smaller overall 75% size profile of this Blackwidow has no impact on the great feel of typing – a clear highlight for the unit. The customizable, colored backlights are also a big selling point, as is the side command dial and built-in OLED display, which can be tweaked to show PC performance, GIFs, lighting brightness, and more. It’s a strong contender in a crowded field, and justifies its price with both comfort and customizability. $300

Beautiful, vibrant art and a refreshing take on the classic area-control board game genre are the two strongest reasons to take a close look at Wroth. Players control one of five races vying for supremacy across a conflict-ridden peninsula. Factions are asymmetric, so everyone has unique capabilities, and that adds significant replayability. Players roll and draft dice, allowing distinct actions that move the game forward. And move it does; unlike many games of this ilk, Wroth can be learned quickly and played to completion in a little over an hour. $65

Console and computer hardware prices are skyrocketing with no sign of slowing, and perhaps as a result, retro gaming handhelds are gaining popularity. Many quality devices are available, but what sets the Evercade Nexus apart is its officially licensed game cartridges. Imagine the nostalgic joy of a Game Boy, but with a cartridge that includes both Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie. The cartridge boxes even include manuals. For fans of physical media, Evercade Nexus is a great option. $199

This tiny USB-C plug-in (with included USB-A adapter) solves a bunch of audio challenges in one uniform device. It offers high-resolution Bluetooth transmission on iPhone, high-bitrate audio transmission to compatible LDAC headphones, enables high-quality Bluetooth output from your PC, and even low-latency Bluetooth audio on PS5 and Switch. In short, it takes a huge number of products with a USB port and ensures a dynamic Bluetooth audio connection with relative ease. $99

The original MV6 is a familiar sight on streams thanks to its clear voice reproduction and overall ease of use. Shure has built on that success with the Gen 2, offering an excellent standalone mic that doesn’t break the bank. Available in black or white, the Gen 2 features a handy auto-level mode that keeps volume even as you adjust your own amplitude, an adjustable denoiser for your space, a longer cable for out-of-the-box convenience, and three presets for plug-and-play use. In short, it’s an excellent choice if you want great performance without needing an audio engineering degree. $169

XR Glasses are still fighting for awareness, but once you try them, it’s easy to see why the concept is on the rise. Viture’s Pro 2 makes an impressive case for adoption, with a competitive price point, comfortable wear, and a giant 146-inch screen that floats in front of your face for gaming or work on your PC or phone. The display is crisp, bright, and impressive, even as the glasses are light and easy to use. With a mobile dock mini (sold separately), you can even snap onto a Switch 2 with ease and start playing instantly. $299

Role-playing gamers have several excellent universal systems to pick between when considering a story or campaign idea that might fall outside traditional genre staples. Among many good options, Cypher stands out as one of the very best. The system uses a rules-light, narrative-focused approach that prioritizes player-driven storytelling across everything from hard sci-fi to superheroes to intrigue- driven espionage. This is the corebook that’s needed to run and play the full system; additional books only add options. $50

As gamers have continually migrated toward personal audio that can rock amazing sound without disturbing the whole house, high-end premium headphones have become a dangerously competitive space. Turtle Beach meets that challenge head-on, with a robust option that sounds beautiful in use. The Stealth Pro II boasts the slick ability to wirelessly switch between different devices, which is awesome if you’re one of those players who regularly jumps between platforms to play your favorite titles. Like the whole category, it’s a lot to spend on a headset, but Dolby Atmos, active noise cancellation, and 60mm dual drivers all add up to a powerful argument. $300

With an increasing number of top-tier console and PC games like Resident Evil Village, No Man’s Sky, and Dead Cells now available on iOS, not to mention the consistent quality of Apple Arcade, Apple phones remain the best mobile platform for gaming. The 18 Pro Max phone has implemented a number of tweaks that strengthen the platform, including higher memory, much faster graphics processing, impressive HDR performance, and notably improved battery life, all adding up to a gaming experience that is working hard to justify your playtime when away from home. Starting at $1299

SteelSeries is best known for its strong audio line-up, but its push into premium-tier controllers exhibits a similar flair for quality and usability. The new Aeon Pro has a lot to recommend it as your go-to Xbox, PC, or mobile choice. The two included batteries (one of which can always be charging in the dock) ensure essentially unlimited playtime. The full-pull or hair triggers and buttons are clicky and satisfying, and the Hall Effect thumbsticks are built to minimize any drift. Textured handgrips and overall heft are ideal. And an onboard OLED lets you adjust profiles and button assignments, switch between platforms, and check battery at a glance. $260

Valve’s pricey VR headset isn’t a revolution in the medium, but the company has been invested in the technology since its inception. As a result, the Steam Frame is a very good, very comfortable headset. Like its competition, the Quest, its best use is playing games locally on the headset, and Steam’s library is vast and interesting. Wireless connected play to a powerful PC is also well done, but currently the included Wireless Adapter is not fully compatible with the Steam Machine – a baffling limitation we were shocked to confirm. VR is an expensive sub-hobby within video games, but Steam Frame is among the best ways to explore and enjoy it. $1059

Many of the coolest “gaming lights” focus on the flexibility and fun of bright RGB customization. While we’re fans of that aesthetic, it leaves others out in the cold who might want something a bit more natural. The Elements hex panels feature a natural wood-inspired panel, customizable “scenes” like a campfire glow, and can react to both music and touch, with adjustable ambient white light to keep the vibe relaxed. $200

Kyle Hilliard contributed to this article.

#4294. The Sims 4 gets a bunch of free items inspired by Coach that you can use right now

As part of a free update, The Sims 4 has kicked off a new collaboration with Coach, which means there's free stuff for everyone.

The Sims 4’s first update of the year is here, though it may not be quite what you might have expected. The game’s latest patch mainly centres around a collaboration with Coach, the luxury fashion brand.

This obviously isn’t the game’s first collaboration with a known brand, though this one does include a lot of free items and accessories that anyone can make use of, even if they don’t care about Coach.

The Coach Collection brings nine new items to The Sims 4. They range from clothes and accessories you can use with Create a Sim, to decoration items available in Build Buy. There’s also The Carriage House, a new Gallery household where you can find three new roommates.

There’s a nice bit of variety in the options available, some casual and others more practical for your Sims to wear. Then there’s The Bag Room, which can also be grabbed from the Gallery. The room simply serves as a way for you to show off your Coach bags and trunks collection.

In case you missed it, The Sims’ development team recently shared an update on some of what we can expect in 2026, both for The Sims 4 as well as other projects currently in the works. It even included further confirmation, if any was needed, that Project Rene is a dedicated mobile off-shoot, and not — as many had long believed — The Sims 5.

The blog post also included a statement about EA’s imminent change of ownership, which many fear could alter the series’ inclusive and diverse nature, and the decisions made by its various teams.

#4293. Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

As larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a new study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.

In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

However, an important question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The new findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue."

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

"Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.

To investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," said Head-Gordon.

The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.

Co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.

"This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts."

By revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a new dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

Materials provided by Columbia University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4291. Cover Reveal – Tomb Raider: Legacy Of Atlantis

Game Informer’s next cover story is Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, the upcoming reimagining of the original 1996 Tomb Raider arriving on February 12. Since that game celebrates the franchise’s 30th anniversary this year, we’re doing the same with a double-whammy of Tomb Raider features.

We visited Crystal Dynamics’ office to play Legacy of Atlantis for several hours, including an exclusive tour of the Greece section. For our 12-page cover story, we spoke to key team members at Crystal Dynamics and Flying Wild Hog to learn why it’s tackling Lara Croft’s seminal adventure once again (having already remade the game once in Tomb Raider: Anniversary), how this version of the game differs from previous incarnations and why, discuss the teams' controversial use of AI development tools, and how Legacy of Atlantis plants seeds for the upcoming Tomb Raider: Catalyst.

The issue also includes a six-page retrospective of Tomb Raider’s 30-year history, with insights from Crystal Dynamics. This celebration is reflected in our cover art, designed by Tomb Raider franchise art director Brenoch Adams, which showcases every version of Lara Croft from the Core Design, Legend, Survivor, and current eras.

The December issue also marks the return of our annual (and very large) holiday buyers guide, featuring curated gift suggestions for the gamers in your life ahead of the winter holidays. Furthermore, we’ve created a list of family-friendly games to enjoy with younger relatives during upcoming holiday gatherings. Guest contributor Veerender Singh Jubbal writes about India's emerging game development scene and how its community is helping elevate local titles to an international stage. Ahead of the launch of Ryu Ga Gatoku’s Stranger Than Heaven, executive editor Brian Shea played a new section of the era-spanning Yakuza/Like a Dragon prequel while picking the brains of its lead designers for details on the game’s plot, themes, and time periods. Senior associate editor Wesley LeBlanc shares his glowing impressions of Murals, the colorful, fairy-tale-inspired adventure from Disney Illusion Island developer Dlala Studios, whom he spoke with about the game’s conception.

We also have plenty of previews for upcoming games including Final Fantasy VII Revelation, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, Muramasa: Revenant Blades, Fate/Extra Record, Tiny Metal 2, Mr. Records, and Eternal Anima. We also have reviews for Gears of War: E-Day, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Control Resonant, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Silent Hill: Downfall, and many more.

#4290. Battlefield 6 Season 2 delayed like many of us expected, but we're getting a new update and a bonus battle pass path

Battlefield 6 has pushed back its next season by nearly a month in order to refine Season 2 content and implement more of players' feedback.

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead announced a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios said that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Escalating the fight with new threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj

What we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension update is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

Similar to other Bonus Paths, the new Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several new customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

EA Sports has revealed the much-anticipated Ultimate Team of the Year cards for the 2025/26 season, including a slew of meta favourites from the likes of the evergreen Virgil van Dijk, super-fast Kylian Mbappe and unplayable queen of FC 26 Claudia Pina.

Elsewhere Lionesses Alessia Russo, Lucy Bronze and Leah Williamson feature alongside now-obligatory Barcelona duo Alexia Putellas and Aitana Bonmati. On the men’s side, Arsenal’s title tilt sees Declan Rice and William Saliba make the first 11, while Champions League holders PSG have the most players from a single team, with Ousmane Dembele, Vitinha and Nuno Mendes adding both rapid speed and technical prowess to proceedings.

However, the Team of the Year selection hasn’t been without controversy. In yet another blow to those of us who got Mario Gomez and Gianluca Vialli from the Classic XI Hero pack, during the TOTY event these Classic XI Heroes will be further upgraded to TOTY Honorable Mentions Heroes.

#4288. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4287. NASA's powerful Moon rocket engine roars through a dramatic 200-second test

NASA has successfully completed another powerful rocket engine test as the agency prepares for future Artemis missions that will return astronauts to the Moon and lay the groundwork for human exploration of Mars.

On November 18, engineers fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 at the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA's Stennis Space Center, located near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. The developmental engine ran for its full scheduled duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds).

Although this particular engine is not intended for spaceflight, the successful test will provide NASA and its primary contractor, L3Harris Technologies, with valuable performance data. Engineers will use the results to improve the power, efficiency, and reliability of RS-25 engines designed for upcoming Artemis missions.

Powerful RS-25 Engines Will Help Send Astronauts Back to the Moon

NASA is preparing for Artemis IV, a mission scheduled for 2028 that aims to land astronauts on the lunar surface. The mission will launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, using the massive Space Launch System (SLS) rocket to carry astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft.

Artemis IV represents an important step toward NASA's larger ambitions. The agency plans to explore the Moon's South Pole, establish a sustained human presence on the lunar surface, and develop the experience and technologies needed for the first crewed journey to Mars.

The RS-25 engines play a crucial role in making these missions possible. Each SLS rocket uses four of the engines, which together generate up to 2 million pounds of thrust to help propel the spacecraft off the launchpad and into space.

Before any RS-25 engine is cleared for flight, it must undergo testing at NASA's Stennis Space Center to verify that it can perform reliably under the extreme conditions of a rocket launch.

These tests are carried out by specialists from NASA, L3Harris Technologies, and Nova Space Solutions, working together to ensure the engines are ready to power future journeys beyond Earth.

#4285. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4284. AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."

A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.

The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.

Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.

Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain

Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.

By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."

A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.

The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

Materials provided by York University. Original written by Sandra McLean. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4280. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.
